name: Pokhara & the Annapurnas
tagline: Lakes, Gurung villages and the Annapurna wall
meta_description: Plan Pokhara and the Annapurnas with locals: Phewa Lake, Poon Hill, Annapurna Base Camp, Ghandruk, Manang, Bandipur and Gorkha, with seasons and permits.
summary: Pokhara and the Annapurnas is Nepal's easiest mountain region to reach and its most varied: a lake city at 822 m, Gurung villages on terraced ridges, teahouse treks to Poon Hill, Mardi Himal and Annapurna Base Camp, the dry Manang valley beyond the range, and the old hill towns of Bandipur and Gorkha.
intro: Few places on earth put a city this close to a wall of ice. From Lakeside in Pokhara, at about 822 m, Machhapuchhre rises to 6,993 m roughly 25 km away, with Annapurna I, Dhaulagiri and Manaslu, three of the world's ten highest peaks, all inside about 50 km. That compression is the whole story of this region: in one day you can drink tea by a lake among banana trees and sleep in a stone village under rhododendron forest.

We split the region into three. Pokhara and its lake valley, with Phewa, Begnas and Rupa lakes, Sarangkot and the ridges above, is the soft base: boats, paragliders, museums and good food. North of it lie the Annapurna trails, where Gurung and Magar villages like Ghandruk, Ghorepani and Chhomrong run teahouses for walkers heading to Poon Hill, Mardi Himal or the Annapurna Sanctuary. Beyond the range, Manang sits in a rain shadow, dry and Tibetan Buddhist.

East of Pokhara, along the Prithvi Highway towards Kathmandu, are two hill towns most visitors drive straight past. Bandipur is a Newar trading bazaar on a saddle, its main street closed to traffic. Gorkha is where the Shah kings began, and where Prithvi Narayan Shah was born in 1723 in the hilltop palace before he set out to unite the hill states into Nepal.

Trips here range from a three-night lake break to sixteen nights on foot. Most of our travellers combine Pokhara with one short trek, then add Bandipur or Gorkha on the road back to Kathmandu. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers inside the Annapurna Conservation Area must walk with a licensed guide; check current status before you travel.

story.title: Kingdoms, caravans and Gurkha villages
paras: Before Nepal was one country these hills were split among the Chaubisi rajya, the twenty-four small kingdoms of the Gandaki basin. Kaski, with its seat at Kaskikot on the ridge west of Pokhara, Lamjung and Tanahun ruled the valleys around the lakes. Gorkha was one of the smallest. Drabya Shah took it in 1559, and his descendant Prithvi Narayan Shah, born in the Gorkha palace in 1723, spent his life absorbing the others, taking Kathmandu in 1768. Kaski itself was folded into the Gorkha state in 1786.

Trade made the towns. Salt, wool and borax came down from Tibet through the Kali Gandaki gorge; grain, cloth and metal went north. Ghorepani, literally 'horse water', was a watering stop for those mule trains. The king of Kaski invited Newar merchant families from Bhaktapur to build a market in Pokhara in the 1770s, and Newars from the same city settled Bandipur on its malaria-free saddle after 1768. Their brick houses and temples still stand in both places.

The hill villages gave the region its other export: soldiers. Gurung and Magar men from Kaski, Lamjung, Syangja and Myagdi have served in British and Indian Gurkha regiments for two centuries, and British Gurkha recruitment selection still runs from a camp in Pokhara. Army pensions built many of the slate-roofed stone houses you will sleep in on the trails, and paid for the schools and water taps beside them.

Modern change came fast. Pokhara had no road until the Siddhartha Highway reached it in 1968; trekkers began arriving soon after, and Lakeside grew from rice fields into a town. In 1986 the Annapurna Conservation Area Project began in Ghandruk with a new idea for Nepal: let villagers manage the forests and the tourism money themselves. Today the area covers 7,629 km2, Nepal's largest protected area, and the villages still sit at its centre.

legend: Local legend says Phewa Lake was once a valley with a rich village. A goddess came disguised as a poor old woman asking for food, and every house turned her away except one poor couple, who shared what little they had. She warned them to flee to higher ground that night. The valley flooded and became the lake, and the goddess, the story goes, is the Barahi honoured in the island temple of Tal Barahi.
people: Gurung people, who call themselves Tamu, fill the high villages from Ghandruk to Sikles; Magar clans, including the Pun of the Ghorepani ridges, hold the western hills. Khas Brahmin and Chhetri farmers work the lower valleys, Newar families keep shops in old Pokhara and Bandipur, and Tibetan Buddhist Manangi people live beyond the range. Four Tibetan refugee settlements around Pokhara date from the 1960s. Farming, army service, remittance and trekking carry most households.

untold.fact: Pokhara Valley's gravels came from catastrophe. Researchers have dated megaflood and landslide deposits from the Sabche Cirque and Annapurna IV to medieval times, around the 11th to 14th centuries, and one 2023 study links up to 23 km3 of material to a single collapse around 1190 AD.

Machhapuchhre has never been officially climbed. A 1957 British team led by Jimmy Roberts stopped about 46 m below the summit by agreement with King Mahendra, and Nepal has issued no permits for the peak since.

The Annapurna Sanctuary was not entered by outsiders until 1956, when Colonel Jimmy Roberts pushed up the Modi Khola gorge between Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre while scouting the next year's attempt on the fishtail peak.
In 2016 nine lakes of the Pokhara Valley, including Phewa, Begnas and Rupa, were listed together as a single Ramsar wetland of international importance, covering about 261 km2 with their catchments.

untold.fact: Manang district gets the lowest rainfall of any district in Nepal because the Annapurna range blocks the monsoon, which is why the Manang side of the Annapurna Circuit stays walkable in summer.

taste.name: Thakali khana set
taste.text: Dal, rice, buckwheat or millet dhido, gundruk, local greens, pickles and ghee, refilled until you stop the cook. The set comes from the Thakali traders of the Kali Gandaki, and Lakeside and the Pokhara bus parks have dozens of Thakali kitchens. On the trails, the same plate becomes plain dal bhat.

highlights.title: Phewa Lake and Tal Barahi
highlights.text: Rent a painted wooden doonga at Barahi Ghat and row ten minutes to the island temple of Tal Barahi. On a clear October morning Machhapuchhre sits upside down in the water. Saturdays bring crowds of local devotees with offerings.

highlights.title: Sunrise from Poon Hill
highlights.text: A pre-dawn climb of about 340 m from Ghorepani puts you at 3,210 m as first light hits Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I. In late March the trail climbs through red and pink rhododendron forest.

highlights.title: Inside the Annapurna Sanctuary
highlights.text: Walk up the Modi Khola gorge into a glacial bowl at 4,130 m, ringed by Annapurna I, Annapurna South, Hiunchuli, Gangapurna and Machhapuchhre. Gurung tradition long treated the sanctuary as the home of gods.

highlights.title: Gurung life in Ghandruk
highlights.text: Stone houses, slate roofs and terraced millet above the Modi Khola: Ghandruk is one of the largest Gurung villages in Nepal and the place where the Annapurna Conservation Area Project began in 1986.

highlights.title: Bandipur's car-free bazaar
highlights.text: A Newar trading street on a 1,030 m saddle, with carved windows, a Rana-era library and views from Dhaulagiri to Langtang on a clear day. Vehicles stay at the edge of town, so evenings are quiet.

highlights.title: Gorkha Durbar on its ridge
highlights.text: Climb from Gorkha bazaar to the palace where Prithvi Narayan Shah was born, with the Kalika temple, the cave of Gorakhnath and views of Manaslu and Himalchuli from the walls.

getting_there: Pokhara is about 200 km west of Kathmandu along the Prithvi Highway. By road it takes 6–8 hours by private car or tourist bus, longer when the highway is under repair near Mugling, which it often is. Flights take about 25 minutes and land at Pokhara International Airport (PHH), opened on 1 January 2023; the old airport still handles Jomsom flights. Tourist buses leave Kathmandu early each morning and arrive at the Tourist Bus Park near Lakeside. Bandipur sits 8 km up a side road from Dumre on the same highway, and Gorkha 24 km up from Abu Khaireni, so both fit naturally into the drive. Trek trailheads such as Nayapul, Kimche, Phedi and Kande are 1–2 hours from Pokhara by jeep.
permits: No permit is needed for Pokhara, Sarangkot, Begnas, Bandipur or Gorkha. Treks to Ghandruk, Poon Hill, Mardi Himal, Annapurna Base Camp and Manang need an Annapurna Conservation Area permit, as we understand it NPR 3,000 for most foreigners and NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals, plus a TIMS card. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers must walk with a licensed guide. Permits are issued in Kathmandu and Pokhara, and checked at posts such as Birethanti. Check current status before you travel.

months.summary: Cold nights and mostly clear skies. Pokhara is pleasant in the sun and the lake is calm, so it is a good month for Sarangkot sunrises and lake days. Low treks such as Ghandruk and Poon Hill are open but Ghorepani can have snow, and Annapurna Base Camp sees deep snow and avalanche risk above Deurali. Thorong La is often closed and many Manang lodges shut. Bandipur and Gorkha are dry and quiet.
months.tip: Pack a warm layer for dawn on Sarangkot, where it can be near freezing.

months.summary: Days warm up and the haze has not yet built, so mountain views are often sharp. Lower rhododendron trees begin to flower by the end of the month. Short treks to Ghandruk, Panchase and Poon Hill work well with fewer walkers than in spring. High routes still carry snow, and the Manang side of the circuit is cold, with Thorong La crossings depending on recent snowfall.
months.tip: Book Ghorepani lodges early on weekends, when Nepali groups also walk.

months.summary: Rhododendron season. The forests between Ghorepani, Deurali and Tadapani turn red, pink and white from mid-March, and Mardi Himal's ridge is at its most colourful. Mountain views are best in the morning before haze rises. Thorong La normally opens for crossings from Manang. It is busy on Poon Hill, so start early.
months.tip: Climb Poon Hill at least 45 minutes before sunrise to find room on the viewing platform.

months.summary: Warm in Pokhara, ideal on the trails, with rhododendrons still flowering higher up. Afternoon thunderstorms become more common by the end of the month. Nepali New Year falls in mid-April and many families travel. Annapurna Base Camp is busy and comfortable, Manang and Thorong La are at their best for spring crossings.
months.tip: Plan walking days to finish by early afternoon, before storms build.

months.summary: Hot and hazy in the valley, with views mainly at dawn. The high trails are still good, especially Manang and the upper Annapurna Sanctuary, but lower sections are sticky and leeches appear late in the month. Pokhara's lakes are warm for paddling. Prices drop and lodges are quieter.
months.tip: Carry a rain shell from mid-May, the monsoon can arrive early.

months.summary: The monsoon usually arrives in the second week of June. Pokhara is one of the wettest cities in Nepal and views are rare. Trails south of the range turn muddy and leeches are everywhere; landslides close roads. The exception is Manang, in the rain shadow, which stays drier, though the road up the Marsyangdi is often blocked.
months.tip: If you trek now, keep two spare days for road closures.

months.summary: Peak monsoon. Rice planting fills the terraces around Begnas and Rupa lakes and the hills are very green, but mountains hide behind cloud for days. Seti river runs high and fast through its gorge. Pokhara works for museums, cafes and lake mornings between showers. We do not recommend southern Annapurna treks this month.
months.tip: Watch rice planting near Begnas, villagers welcome photos if you ask first.

months.summary: Still monsoon, with frequent landslides on the Prithvi Highway and trekking roads. Flights between Kathmandu and Pokhara are the reliable link. Bandipur and Gorkha are wet but walkable in gaps between rain, with lush terraces and few visitors. Manang is the only trek we suggest, approached with spare days.
months.tip: Book the flight rather than the bus when highway landslides are reported.

months.summary: Rain eases through the month and views return in the last week. Trails are green and quiet, with some mud. Dashain, Nepal's biggest festival, often begins in late September or October; the Phulpati procession carries sacred items from Gorkha towards Kathmandu. Book transport early around Dashain, when Nepalis travel home.
months.tip: Start treks from the third week of September for the best chance of clear mornings.

months.summary: The best month for mountain views: rain-washed air, warm days and cold, starry nights. Every Annapurna trek is open, rice is ripening gold on the terraces and Dashain and Tihar fill the villages with swings, kites and family visits. It is also the busiest month on the trails, so lodges and flights must be booked early.
months.tip: Reserve Pokhara flights and trek lodges at least six weeks ahead.

months.summary: Clear, stable weather and slightly fewer people than October. High camps are cold at night, around -10 °C at Annapurna Base Camp by the end of the month. It is a fine month for Thorong La and for the views from Bandipur and Gorkha, where the snow peaks stand clear from Dhaulagiri to Ganesh Himal.
months.tip: Bring a four-season sleeping bag for anything above 3,500 m.

months.summary: Short days, clear skies and quiet trails. Pokhara gets festive at year's end with the Pokhara Street Festival along Lakeside, and Gurung families celebrate Tamu Lhosar, their new year, around 30 December. Low treks are good; high routes are cold and Thorong La can close after snowfall.
months.tip: Join Tamu Lhosar gatherings in Pokhara to see Gurung dress and dances.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Pokhara and the Annapurnas?
faqs.a: Plan at least five nights: two in Pokhara and a three-night Poon Hill or Ghandruk loop. Annapurna Base Camp needs 7–10 nights from Pokhara, Mardi Himal 4–6, and the Annapurna Circuit through Manang 12–16. Add a night each in Bandipur and Gorkha on the way to or from Kathmandu. With two weeks you can do one proper trek and the hill towns without rushing.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to trek in the Annapurna region?
faqs.a: Yes, as we understand the rules. Since April 2023 Nepal requires foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas, including the Annapurna Conservation Area, to trek with a licensed guide, and checkpoints such as Birethanti ask to see one. Indian nationals have been treated differently at times. Rules and enforcement have changed several times, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What permits are needed for Annapurna treks?
faqs.a: You need an Annapurna Conservation Area permit, as we understand it NPR 3,000 for most foreigners and NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals, and a TIMS card. Both are issued in Kathmandu at the Nepal Tourism Board office and in Pokhara, usually by your trekking company. Keep them handy for checkpoints. No permit is needed for Pokhara, Sarangkot, Begnas, Bandipur or Gorkha. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Pokhara?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest mountain views and dry trails; March and April bring rhododendron blossom and warm days with some haze. December to February are cold at dawn but often clear. June to September is monsoon: Pokhara is among Nepal's wettest places, views are rare and leeches are common on lower trails, though Manang stays drier in the rain shadow.

faqs.q: Should I fly or drive from Kathmandu to Pokhara?
faqs.a: Fly if time is short or in monsoon: the flight takes about 25 minutes to Pokhara International Airport. Drive if you want to stop at Bandipur, Gorkha or the Manakamana cable car: the 200 km road takes 6–8 hours, sometimes more around Mugling. Tourist buses are cheap and comfortable enough; a private car lets you stop for river views and fish lunches.

faqs.q: Which is the easiest Annapurna trek?
faqs.a: The Ghorepani Poon Hill loop, 3–4 nights from Pokhara, is the easiest with big views: highest point 3,210 m, good lodges, and roads at both ends. Ghandruk alone is easier still, two nights. Panchase is a quieter low option at 2,517 m. All involve steep stone steps, so some fitness helps. Mardi Himal and Annapurna Base Camp go higher and need more days.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk on Annapurna treks?
faqs.a: Poon Hill (3,210 m) and Ghandruk carry little risk for healthy walkers. Mardi Himal High Camp (3,580 m), Annapurna Base Camp (4,130 m) and Manang (3,519 m) are high enough for symptoms. Climb steadily, drink water, avoid alcohol and descend if headache, vomiting or confusion worsen. In Manang an aid post run by the Himalayan Rescue Association gives altitude talks during the trekking seasons.

faqs.q: Can Indian travellers visit Pokhara without a passport?
faqs.a: Indian citizens can enter Nepal with a valid passport or a voter ID card and do not need a visa. For Annapurna treks they pay the SAARC permit rate. Hotels in Pokhara will ask for identification at check-in, and flights need a valid photo ID. Large-denomination Indian rupee notes have faced restrictions in Nepal at times, so carry smaller notes and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Pokhara good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. Lakeside is flat and walkable, boats on Phewa are calm and inexpensive, and the International Mountain Museum, Davis Falls and Gupteshwor cave suit children. Sarangkot sunrise is a short drive. For a first walk, a two-night Ghandruk trip or a day at Australian Camp gives village life without long climbs. Avoid the monsoon months, when trails and roads are slippery.
